NON-STEROIDAL ANTI-INFLAMMATORY DRUGS (NSAIDS)
• NSAIDs are among the most widely used of all
agents. Available over the counter, they are used to
treat minor aches and pains.
• Chemically unrelated
• Despite diversity all the NSAIDs possess analgesic, Ibuprofen
antipyretic and anti-inflammatory properties
• They share to varying degrees the same adverse reactions
• Other examples:
― Diclofenac (Voltaren) Celecoxib

NSAIDs - Pharmacodynamics
WHAT THE DRUGS DO TO THE BODY AND HOW THEY DO IT
• Analgesic effect
― Decreased production of prostaglandin: less
sensitisation of nociceptive nerve ending to
inflammatory mediators such as bradykinin
and 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT, serotonin)
• Anti-inflammatory action
― Reduces vasodilation and, indirectly, oedema
by decreasing prostaglandin E and
2
prostacyclin synthesis
• Antipyretic effect
― NSAIDs prevents the release of
prostaglandins by interleukin-1 in the CNS,
where prostaglandins elevate the
hypothalamic set point for temperature
control. Therefore preventing fever

NSAIDs
PHARMACOKINETICS
• Route of administration – topical, enteral and
parenteral
• Site of absorption – stomach and small intestine
(presence of food and antacids delays
absorption)
• Distribution – highly bound to plasma protein.
Wide spread including breast milk and cross
placenta (most)
• Metabolism – Liver (main)
• Excretion – Kidneys (main)

Paracetamol
WHERE DOES IT FIT?

Paracetamol
ACETAMINOPHEN
• Paracetamol has analgesic and antipyretic properties
• Very weak (negligible) anti-inflammatory effects – not
suitable substitute for NSAIDs in chronic inflammatory
conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis
• Mechanism of action widely studied but still not well
understood. Proposed inhibition of COX isoform mainly
available at the CNS, however alternative explanations
have been proposed
• Well tolerated and low incidence of GI side effects
• Acute overdose can cause severe hepatic damage
